claim: SLC1A5 (ASCT2) is the primary transporter of glutamine in cancer cells.
source: Alanine-serine-cysteine transporter 2 (ASCT2, SLC1A5) is the primary transporter of glutamine in cancer cells and regulates the mTORC1 signaling pathway.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: SLC1A5 regulates the mTORC1 signaling pathway.
source: Alanine-serine-cysteine transporter 2 (ASCT2, SLC1A5) is the primary transporter of glutamine in cancer cells and regulates the mTORC1 signaling pathway.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The cryo-EM structures of human SLC1A5 were determined in an outward-facing conformation.
source: Here, we present cryo-EM structures of human SLC1A5 and its complex with the substrate, L-glutamine in an outward-facing conformation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data including resolution values and structural analysis.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of SLC1A5 in complex with L-glutamine was determined at 3.8 Å resolution.
source: To gain insights into structural features that permit substrate recognition in an outward-facing state, using an antibody fragment as a fiducial marker we have solved the cryo-EM structures of the unliganded transporter and its complex with glutamine at 3.5 and 3.8 Å resolution, respectively.
evidence: This is directly stated in the introduction and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of unliganded SLC1A5 was determined at 3.5 Å resolution.
source: To gain insights into structural features that permit substrate recognition in an outward-facing state, using an antibody fragment as a fiducial marker we have solved the cryo-EM structures of the unliganded transporter and its complex with glutamine at 3.5 and 3.8 Å resolution, respectively.
evidence: This is directly stated in the introduction and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: The ECL2a loop connects the transport domain and scaffold domain.
source: These structures reveal insights into the conformation of the critical ECL2a loop which connects the two domains, thus allowing rigid body movement of the transport domain throughout the transport cycle.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis in the results section.

claim: Substrate recognition involves conformational changes in the HP2 loop.
source: Furthermore, the structures provide new insights into substrate recognition, which involves conformational changes in the HP2 loop.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural data showing HP2 loop conformational changes upon substrate binding.

claim: A putative cholesterol binding site was observed near the domain interface in the outward-facing state.
source: A putative cholesterol binding site was observed near the domain interface in the outward-facing state.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cryo-EM density and mass spectrometry data.

claim: SLC1A5 catalyzes an obligatory Na+-dependent antiport in which Na+ together with an extracellular neutral amino acid are exchanged with an intracellular neutral amino acid.
source: SLC1A5 (ASCT2) catalyzes an obligatory Na+-dependent antiport in which Na+ together with an extracellular neutral amino acid are exchanged with an intracellular neutral amino acid (Kanai and Hediger, 2004; Utsunomiya-Tate et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: SLC1A5 is the only member of the SLC1 sub-family that is competent to transport glutamine.
source: Among the solute carrier family 1 (SLC1) sub-family, it is the only one that is competent to transport glutamine, and it serves as the primary transporter of glutamine in cancer cells (Fuchs and Bode, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Inhibition of SLC1A5 glutamine transport by small molecules and shRNA-mediated SLC1A5 knockdown decrease endometrial cancer cell growth.
source: Inhibition of SLC1A5 glutamine transport by small molecules and shRNA-mediated SLC1A5 knockdown have been shown to decrease endometrial cancer cell growth (Marshall et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: SLC1A5 inhibition and knockdown suppressed mTORC1 signaling and induced rapid cell death in breast cancer cells.
source: Similarly, SLC1A5 inhibition and knockdown suppressed mTORC1 signaling and induced rapid cell death in breast cancer cells (van Geldermalsen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: SLC1A5 -/- mice are deficient in T cell receptor-mediated activation of the metabolic kinase mTORC1.
source: In addition, SLC1A5 -/- mice are deficient in T cell receptor-mediated activation of the metabolic kinase mTORC1 and as a result exhibit improved clinical scores in experimental autoimmune animal models of multiple sclerosis and colitis (Nakaya et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: SLC1 transporters form a trimer of independently functioning protomers.
source: All these transporters form a trimer of independently functioning protomers that uses an elevator mechanism to carry amino acids across membranes (Akyuz et al., 2015; Erkens et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Each protomer of SLC1 transporters has a scaffold domain and a movable transport domain which slides and carries the solute.
source: Each protomer has a scaffold domain and a movable transport domain which slides and carries the solute.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by structural data.

claim: GltPH structures have been reported in both the outward- and the inward-facing states.
source: GltPH structures have been reported in both the outward- and the inward-facing states (Boudker et al., 2007; Reyes et al., 2009; Akyuz et al., 2015; Verdon et al., 2014; Verdon and Boudker, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Crystal structures of unbound and substrate-bound GltTK have been reported in the outward-facing conformation.
source: Crystal structures of unbound and substrate-bound GltTK have also been reported in the outward-facing conformation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: Crystal structures of SLC1A3 were determined with competitive and allosteric inhibitors in the outward-facing conformation.
source: The crystal structures of SLC1A3 were determined with competitive and allosteric inhibitors in the outward-facing conformation (Canul-Tec et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Crystallographic studies of SLC1A3 required mutation of nearly 25% of its primary sequence.
source: Crystallographic studies of SLC1A3 required mutation of nearly 25% of its primary sequence suggesting the inherent technical challenges with this gene family (Canul-Tec et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Cryo-EM structures of SLC1A5 in complex with glutamine or inhibitor were reported in the inward-facing state.
source: Recently, the cryo-EM structures of SLC1A5 in complex with glutamine or inhibitor were reported in the inward-facing state (Garaeva et al., 2018; Garaeva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Full-length SLC1A5 construct showed high expression and stability.
source: Our full-length SLC1A5 construct showed high expression and stability. (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by figure data.

claim: The presence of affinity tags used for purification did not affect the sodium-dependent glutamine uptake when HAP1 SLC1A5 knock-out cells were transiently transfected with full-length SLC1A5.
source: The presence of affinity tags used for purification did not affect the sodium-dependent glutamine uptake when HAP1 SLC1A5 knock-out cells were transiently transfected with full-length SLC1A5 but the observed transport activity was low, compared to the background.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by experimental data.

claim: The observed transport activity of full-length SLC1A5 was low, compared to the background.
source: The presence of affinity tags used for purification did not affect the sodium-dependent glutamine uptake when HAP1 SLC1A5 knock-out cells were transiently transfected with full-length SLC1A5 but the observed transport activity was low, compared to the background.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by experimental data.

claim: A cKM4012 Fab fragment was used to assist structural determination of SLC1A5.
source: To assist structural determination, we generated its complex with a commercially available cKM4012 Fab fragment.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: KM4012 antibody isolated through a cell-based screen inhibited glutamine-dependent cancer cell growth.
source: It is reported that KM4012 antibody isolated through a cell-based screen inhibited glutamine-dependent cancer cell growth (Suzuki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The purpose of the Fab was to serve as a fiducial marker for particle alignment.
source: The purpose of the Fab was to serve as a fiducial marker for particle alignment.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the results section.

claim: Negative-stain electron microscopy revealed that one molecule of Fab was bound to each protomer of a SLC1A5 homotrimer.
source: Negative-stain electron microscopy revealed that one molecule of Fab was bound to each protomer of a SLC1A5 homotrimer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by figure data.

claim: The three-fold symmetry of SLC1A5 was broken due to the dynamic nature of each Fab and protomer.
source: The three-fold symmetry was broken due to the dynamic nature of each Fab and protomer.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and inferred from structural analysis.

claim: Single-particle electron cryo-microscopy analysis without imposing any symmetry restraint resulted in a three-dimensional reconstruction at an overall resolution of 3.5 Å.
source: Single-particle electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM) analysis without imposing any symmetry restraint resulted in a facile three-dimensional reconstruction at an overall resolution of 3.5 Å (Fourier shell correlation (FSC) = 0.143 criterion; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by FSC data.

claim: The highly flexible Fab fragments were masked out to maximize the structural quality of SLC1A5.
source: The highly flexible Fab fragments were masked out to maximize the structural quality of SLC1A5 (Figure 1—figure supplements 2,3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by figure data.

claim: The quality of the EM density map was sufficient to allow model building for residues 43–488.
source: The quality of the EM density map was sufficient to allow model building for residues 43–488 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by figure and table data.

claim: The structure of SLC1A5 shows a homotrimer with an overall GltPH-like fold in an outward-facing conformation.
source: The structure of SLC1A5 shows a homotrimer with an overall GltPH-like fold in an outward-facing conformation, Each SLC1A5 protomer contains two domains, a transport domain and a scaffold domain connected by the extracellular loop region 2 (ECL2a and ECL2b) (Figure 1a-c, Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: Each SLC1A5 protomer contains two domains: a transport domain and a scaffold domain connected by the extracellular loop region 2 (ECL2a and ECL2b).
source: The structure of SLC1A5 shows a homotrimer with an overall GltPH-like fold in an outward-facing conformation, Each SLC1A5 protomer contains two domains, a transport domain and a scaffold domain connected by the extracellular loop region 2 (ECL2a and ECL2b) (Figure 1a-c, Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The individual transport domain containing transmembrane helices TM3, TM6-TM8 and helical loops 1–2 (HP1-HP2) interacts exclusively with the scaffold domain from its own protomer.
source: The individual transport domain containing transmembrane helices TM3, TM6-TM8 and helical loops 1–2 (HP1-HP2) interacts exclusively with the scaffold domain from its own protomer.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural analysis.

claim: The scaffold domain including TM1-TM2 and TM4-TM5 is involved in inter-protomer interactions and forms a compact core.
source: The scaffold domain including TM1-TM2 and TM4-TM5 is involved in inter-protomer interactions and forms a compact core.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural analysis.

claim: ECL2 connects TM3 to TM5 via TM4 and bridges the two domains.
source: The ECL2 connects TM3 to TM5 via TM4 and bridges the two domains.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural analysis.

claim: ECL2a spans about 55 Å across a quarter of the transport domain, sequentially interacting with ECL3, TM8, TM7a, and HP2b on extracellular surface.
source: ECL2a spans about 55 Å across a quarter of the transport domain, sequentially interacting with ECL3, TM8, TM7a, and HP2b on extracellular surface.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural measurements.

claim: Superposition with the inward-facing state demonstrates that the scaffold domain remains relatively rigid, while the transport domain moves toward the cytoplasm.
source: Superposition with the inward-facing state demonstrates that the scaffold domain remains relatively rigid, while the transport domain moves toward the cytoplasm and the substrate binding site shifts by 19 Å toward the cytoplasmic face (Figure 2a-b) (Garaeva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The substrate binding site shifts by 19 Å toward the cytoplasmic face during the transition from outward-facing to inward-facing state.
source: Superposition with the inward-facing state demonstrates that the scaffold domain remains relatively rigid, while the transport domain moves toward the cytoplasm and the substrate binding site shifts by 19 Å toward the cytoplasmic face (Figure 2a-b) (Garaeva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural comparison data.

claim: ECL3 possesses one α-helix with ~1.5 turns that connects TM6 to TM5 of the scaffold domain in the outward-facing state.
source: The ECL3 possessing one α-helix with ~1.5 turns connects the TM6 to the TM5 of the scaffold domain in the outward-facing state (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: In the inward-facing state, the 1.5 turn α-helix in ECL3 merges into TM6 which extends the length of TM6 by about 9.5 Å.
source: In the inward-facing state (PDB: 6GCT), this 1.5 turn α-helix in ECL3 merges into TM6 which extends the length of TM6 by about 9.5 Å (Figure 2a,c) (Garaeva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The N-terminus of TM3 unwinds by approximately 1.5 turns and extends the TM2-3 loop in the cytoplasmic space during the transition to the inward-facing state.
source: Simultaneously, to compensate the movement of the transport domain and the conformational changes of TM6, the N-terminus of TM3 unwinds by approximately 1.5 turns and extends the TM2-3 loop in the cytoplasmic space (Figure 2b–c).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The extension of TM2-3 loop increases the distance between TM2 and TM3, resulting in a ~ 20° tilt compared to the outward-facing state.
source: The extension of TM2-3 loop increases the distance between TM2 and TM3, resulting in a ~ 20° tilt compared to the outward-facing state (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The structurally symmetrical TM3 and TM6 serve as a platform which holds the core region of the transport domain.
source: The structurally symmetrical TM3 and TM6 serve as a platform which holds the core region of the transport domain (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural analysis.

claim: The movement of the transport domain is coupled with a ~ 30° rotation during the transition between outward- and inward-facing states.
source: During the transition between outward- and inward-facing states, the changes in lengths of the TM3, TM2-3 loop, TM6 and ECL3 regions trigger the adjustment in the platform plane relative to the membrane plane, resulting in the movement of the transport domain coupled with a ~ 30° rotation (Figure 2a-c) (Garaeva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The well-defined ECL2a undergoes a large conformational rearrangement, swinging out by ~35° relative to the transport domain when compared with an inward-facing state of a cross-linked GltPH structure.
source: Notably, the well-defined ECL2a undergoes a large conformational rearrangement, swinging out by ~35° relative to the transport domain when compared with an inward-facing state of a cross-linked GltPH structure (Figure 2d) (Reyes et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural comparison data.

claim: In the outward-facing state, ECL2a encompasses one side of the transport domain and is positioned to expose both the ECL4 and ECL5.
source: In the outward-facing state, the ECL2a encompasses one side of the transport domain and is positioned to expose both the ECL4 and ECL5.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural analysis.

claim: In the inward-facing state, ECL2a forms a sharp turn and sits on top of the transport domain covering a narrow groove formed by the ECL4 and ECL5.
source: However, in the inward-facing state, the ECL2a forms a sharp turn and sits on top of the transport domain covering a narrow groove formed by the ECL4 and ECL5 to accommodate rigid body movement of the transport domain (Reyes et al., 2009; Verdon et al., 2014; Verdon and Boudker, 2012; Reyes et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations.

claim: The density was sufficient to dock the L-Gln molecule in the substrate-bound structure.
source: The density was sufficient to dock the L-Gln molecule (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by figure data.

claim: The Gln binding pocket is formed by two oppositely oriented reentrant loops (HP1 and HP2), TM7 and TM8 of the transport domain.
source: The Gln binding pocket is formed by two oppositely oriented reentrant loops (HP1 and HP2), TM7 and TM8 of the transport domain (Figure 3a–b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The HP2 loop in the unliganded structure is in an open conformation providing a direct access to the binding site.
source: The HP2 loop in the unliganded structure is in an open conformation providing a direct access to the binding site.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: Upon Gln binding, HP2 loop acts as a gatekeeper and comes close to the serine-rich HP1 loop to shield the substrate from the extracellular surface.
source: Upon Gln binding, HP2 loop acts as a gatekeeper and comes close to the serine-rich HP1 loop to shield the substrate from the extracellular surface (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The substrate binding interaction is maintained between the outward-facing and inward-facing states of SLC1A5.
source: Furthermore, the substrate binding interaction is maintained between the two states of SLC1A5 (Figure 3c) (Garaeva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural comparison data.

claim: Both α-amino and α-carboxylate groups of the substrate appear to be anchored by the carbonyl backbone of Ser351, the amide backbone and the sidechain of Ser353 in the HP1 loop.
source: Both α-amino and α-carboxylate groups of the substrate appear to be anchored by the carbonyl backbone of Ser351, the amide backbone and the sidechain of Ser353 in the HP1 loop and can be further stabilized by sidechains of Asp464 and Asn471 in TM8 (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The Nε2 of the substrate, L-Gln, is within hydrogen bond distance to the sidechain of Asp464 in TM8.
source: Importantly, the Nε2 of the substrate, L-Gln, is within hydrogen bond distance to the sidechain of Asp464 in TM8.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: A smaller substrate, L-Asn, could fit into the binding site to satisfy the interaction with Asp464.
source: A smaller substrate, L-Asn, could fit into the binding site to satisfy the interaction with Asp464, consistent with the comparable Km values of human SLC1A5 for L-Asn and L-Gln determined in proteoliposomes (Scalise et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by inference from structural data and citation.

claim: The position of L-Gln in the SLC1A5 structure is similar to that of the L-Asp in the SLC1A3 crystal structure.
source: The position of L-Gln in our SLC1A5 structure is similar to that of the L-Asp in the SLC1A3 crystal structure, suggesting a conserved-ligand binding pocket among SLC1 family members (Figure 3d) (Yernool et al., 2004; Canul-Tec et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural comparison data.

claim: Cys467 is a unique residue among the SLC1 family.
source: Cys467, a unique residue among the SLC1 family, is at a suitable distance to donate its proton to the carbonyl group of the Gln substrate (Figure 3b, Figure 1—figure supplement 5) and could thus contribute to substrate selectivity.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data and sequence alignment.

claim: Cys467 is at a suitable distance to donate its proton to the carbonyl group of the Gln substrate.
source: Cys467, a unique residue among the SLC1 family, is at a suitable distance to donate its proton to the carbonyl group of the Gln substrate (Figure 3b, Figure 1—figure supplement 5) and could thus contribute to substrate selectivity.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: Mutation of Cys467 to Ala in SLC1A5 showed significant increase in Km for Gln.
source: Mutation of Cys467 to Ala in SLC1A5 showed significant increase in Km for Gln (Scalise et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The corresponding residue to Cys467 in all glutamate transporters of the SLC1 family is a conserved bulkier Arg residue.
source: The corresponding residue in all glutamate transporters of the SLC1 family is a conserved bulkier Arg residue (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: In SLC1A3, the Arg residue with its guanidinium group forms a hydrogen bond with the carboxylate group of the substrate Asp.
source: In SLC1A3, the Arg residue with its guanidinium group forms a hydrogen bond with the carboxylate group of the substrate Asp, and a favorable cation-π interaction with a Tyr residue (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: SLC1A5 has an additional side cavity involving Phe393, Val436, Ala433, Val463 and Asp464 as a result of the smaller amino acid at position 467.
source: As a result of the smaller amino acid at this location, SLC1A5 has an additional side cavity involving Phe393, Val436, Ala433, Val463 and Asp464, whereas no such cavity is present in SLC1A3 (Figure 3b,d).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural comparison data.

claim: No such cavity is present in SLC1A3.
source: As a result of the smaller amino acid at this location, SLC1A5 has an additional side cavity involving Phe393, Val436, Ala433, Val463 and Asp464, whereas no such cavity is present in SLC1A3 (Figure 3b,d).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural comparison data.

claim: An equivalent mutation of threonine in SLC1A4 (Thr459) to a cysteine resulted in alteration to L-Gln binding.
source: The critical role of the Cys467 in SLC1A5 for substrate specificity was further supported by an equivalent mutation of threonine in SLC1A4 (Thr459) to a cysteine, resulting in alteration to L-Gln binding (Scopelliti et al., 2018) and inhibition by Cys modifying reagents in proteoliposome assays (Pingitore et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: Ala390 is a conserved residue in neutral amino acid transporters, SLC1A4 and SLC1A5.
source: Ala390, a conserved residue in neutral amino acid transporters, SLC1A4 and SLC1A5, does not form any contact with the Gln substrate and could tolerate small neutral amino acid substrates (Figure 3b, Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data and sequence alignment.

claim: Ala390 does not form any contact with the Gln substrate and could tolerate small neutral amino acid substrates.
source: Ala390, a conserved residue in neutral amino acid transporters, SLC1A4 and SLC1A5, does not form any contact with the Gln substrate and could tolerate small neutral amino acid substrates (Figure 3b, Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The structurally equivalent residue to Ala390 in SLC1A3 is Thr which forms a hydrogen bond with the carboxylate group of the substrate.
source: In contrast, the structurally equivalent residue Thr in SLC1A3 forms a hydrogen bond with the carboxylate group of the substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural comparison.

claim: Stretches of residual EM densities were observed in a hydrophobic crevice near the domain interface in the presence or absence of glutamine.
source: Stretches of residual EM densities were observed in a hydrophobic crevice near the domain interface in the presence or absence of glutamine (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by figure data.

claim: Based on the shape of the density and the presence of cholesteryl hemisuccinate (CHS) during purification, the residual EM density was assigned to CHS.
source: Based on the shape of the density and the presence of cholesteryl hemisuccinate (CHS) during purification, we assigned this density to CHS.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by inference from density shape and purification conditions.

claim: Using an unbiased lipidomics approach, CHS was detected as a major component in the sample used for cryo-EM.
source: Using an unbiased lipidomics approach, CHS was detected as a major component in the sample used for cryo-EM.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by lipidomics data.

claim: The identity of CHS was confirmed by mass spectrometry using commercially available CHS as a reference.
source: The identity of CHS was further confirmed by mass spectrometry using commercially available CHS as a reference (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: The cryo-EM density supports a specific binding site for CHS in the outward-facing SLC1A5 conformation.
source: The cryo-EM density supports a specific binding site for CHS in the outward-facing SLC1A5 conformation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by density data.

claim: CHS binds inside a hydrophobic pocket formed by TM3, TM4a, TM4c and TM7 from one protomer, as well as TM5 from the adjacent protomer.
source: Electron density suggests that CHS binds inside a hydrophobic pocket formed by TM3, TM4a, TM4c and TM7 from one protomer, as well as TM5 from the adjacent protomer (Figure 3—figure supplements 2,3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by density data.

claim: The putative lipid density was also observed in the inward-facing state of SLC1A5.
source: The putative lipid density was also observed in the inward-facing state of SLC1A5, located in a hydrophobic pocket formed by TM3, TM4a, TM4c, and HP2a from one protomer, and TM5 from the adjacent protomer (Garaeva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The specific CHS-binding site in SLC1A5 overlaps with the UCPH101 allosteric binding site reported in SLC1A3 structure.
source: Remarkably, the specific CHS-binding site in SLC1A5 overlaps with the UCPH101 allosteric binding site reported in SLC1A3 structure (Canul-Tec et al., 2017) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The highly lipophilic UCPH101 binds in the outward-facing conformation and blocks the movement of the transport domain relative to the scaffold domain.
source: The highly lipophilic UCPH101 binds in the outward-facing conformation and blocks the movement of the transport domain relative to the scaffold domain.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citation.

claim: Additional putative lipid density was reported previously in the inward-facing state of SLC1A5, located between the transport and scaffold domains within the same protomer.
source: Additional putative lipid density was reported previously in the inward-facing state of SLC1A5, located between the transport and scaffold domains within the same protomer (Garaeva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The corresponding density to the additional putative lipid was not observed in the outward-facing state of SLC1A5 due to differences in the local environment between the transport and scaffold domains.
source: The corresponding density was not observed in the outward-facing state of SLC1A5 due to differences in the local environment between the transport and scaffold domains.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural comparison.

claim: Human SLC1A5 is the first eukaryotic sodium-dependent neutral amino acid transporter for which both the inward- and outward-facing conformational states have been mapped by cryo-EM.
source: Human SLC1A5 is the first eukaryotic sodium-dependent neutral amino acid transporter for which both the inward- and outward-facing conformational states have been mapped by cryo-EM.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section.

claim: HP2 is the extracellular gate that controls entry of the substrate.
source: Our cryo-EM structures of unbound and substrate-bound SLC1A5 revealed that HP2 is the extracellular gate that controls entry of the substrate (Boudker et al., 2007; Canul-Tec et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by structural data and citations.

claim: As a gatekeeper, HP2 in the closed conformation is near the serine-rich HP1, shielding the substrate from the extracellular surface.
source: As a gatekeeper, HP2 in the closed conformation is near the serine-rich HP1, shielding the substrate from the extracellular surface (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by structural data.

claim: The structure of the unliganded form of SLC1A5 provides an example for the HP2 loop in an open conformation.
source: The structure of the unliganded form of SLC1A5 provides an example for the HP2 loop in an open conformation and serves as a useful starting model for designing competitive inhibitors such as TBOA (Boudker et al., 2007; Colas et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by structural data.

claim: The opening of the HP2 loop increases the accessible surface area, exposing a previously unidentified cryptic pocket.
source: The opening of the HP2 loop increases the accessible surface area, exposing a previously unidentified cryptic pocket which could accommodate a large inhibitor that could specifically target the open conformation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by structural analysis.

claim: The closed conformation of HP2 has a small binding site, limiting the size of the inhibitors.
source: In contrast, the closed conformation of HP2 has a small binding site, limiting the size of the inhibitors (Colas et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: The human SLC1A5 represents a distinct SLC1 subfamily identifiable in part by the Cys and Ala residues for substrate specificity.
source: The human SLC1A5 represents a distinct SLC1 subfamily identifiable in part by the Cys and Ala residues for substrate specificity and the unique conformation of the two ECL2a and ECL2b loops allowing for structural flexibility at TM4b for the key trimer interaction.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by structural and sequence analysis.

claim: The unique conformation of the two ECL2a and ECL2b loops allows for structural flexibility at TM4b for the key trimer interaction.
